pending_qa.q: How did the Houthis emerge as a major power player in Yemen and what triggered their recent military advances?
pending_qa.r: The Houthis started as a ragtag religious movement in northern Yemen and became increasingly important starting in 2014, when they swept into Sana'a and took over the capital after a failed Arab Spring transition. They remained frustrated by lack of political recognition and access to oil resources, and this frustration collided with Iran's hardliners' interests in escalating pressure on global energy markets during the Iran war.

pending_qa.q: What specific events in July and recent weeks led to the collapse of Saudi Arabia's oil export alternatives?
pending_qa.r: In July, the Houthis declared a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea. Last week, the Houthis pushed towards the Red Sea coast and seized vast territory along Yemen's most strategic real estate, ending up in control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait. On the same Friday they took this territory, Saudi Arabia announced that the crucial east-west pipeline across the kingdom had been attacked and had to be shut down, leaving all exits for Arabian Peninsula oil severely choked off or cut off.

pending_qa.q: Why did the Trump administration decline to intervene militarily against the Houthis despite Saudi Arabia's requests for support?
pending_qa.r: According to Trump's statements, the Houthis don't want to fight the U.S., only Saudi Arabia. Trump has also cited that the U.S. already fought the Houthis in a brief and ill-fated airstrike campaign last year, and no one has found a military solution to them. They have repeatedly forced much wealthier and more powerful foes to back down, so Trump doesn't see getting involved in a war against the Houthis as a winning prospect.

pending_qa.q: What are Saudi Arabia's limited options to address the blockade of all oil export routes?
pending_qa.r: Saudi Arabia's options include going back to war with the Houthis to force them to back down militarily, which didn't go well the first time. Another option is to negotiate a diplomatic solution, but the Houthis have a history of maximalist demands and are unlikely to back down easily now that they feel they have the upper hand. There is also no guarantee a diplomatic agreement would be sustainable.

pending_qa.q: What are the broader economic and humanitarian consequences of the escalating conflict in the region beyond gas prices?
pending_qa.r: Saudi Arabia's entire economy and government budget depend on oil revenue, and their diversification efforts also rely on oil revenue to fund costly investments. If they cannot get oil to global markets, it is an existential problem. Additionally, Yemen is tilting back into full-blown war, which could have devastating consequences for tens of millions of people already living in one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
